payload.title: Bridesmaids Tradition and Where It Comes From
protect_keywords: maid of honour vs matron of honour
how many bridesmaids should I have
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s, planning a wedding overseas with a generous budget, who are deciding who will stand beside them and want to know where the bridesmaid tradition really comes from, what a maid or matron of honour and a bridesman actually do, how many attendants feels right, and how to ask friends to travel for the role with grace before they make the call.
payload.goal: Read the free Wedded Wonderland digital magazine (primary CTA); secondary, in-context invitation to speak with a Wedded Advisor placed after the destination section.
payload.angle: Most pages answer with a tidy story about decoys and evil spirits and move on. We state the bridesmaid's history only where the Royal Collection, royal.uk, the V&A, Britannica or Oxford Reference give it (early references as those sources put them, Queen Victoria's twelve bridesmaids, royal attendants as official pages record them), and otherwise write with confident authority about the role as couples live it now. Then we turn to the decisions a couple marrying abroad actually faces: who to ask and how many, maid or matron of honour, a mixed party with bridesmen, what attendants do before and on the day, how to invite friends to travel for the role and talk openly about costs, and how to thank them. What to wear is left to our bridesmaid attire guide.
must_include: About 10 numbered sections: why we have bridesmaids today; early history as sourced; Victorian and royal bridesmaids; maid or matron of honour; matching dresses (history only); how many bridesmaids; roles before and on the day; mixed wedding parties and bridesmen; bridesmaids at a destination wedding; thanking your bridesmaids

Origins, dates and meanings stated as fact only where Royal Collection Trust, royal.uk, V&A, Britannica or Oxford Reference give them; otherwise confident living practice ('Many couples...'); 'often told' at most once; no myths section; no 'evil spirits' or decoy story unless a reference states it
Royal examples (e.g. Queen Victoria's 1840 bridesmaids) only as rct.uk, royal.uk or the V&A describe them, cited once by link
Maid versus matron of honour defined by Britannica or Oxford Reference if they give it; otherwise as living practice; any partner of any gender, said once

Destination section as practical questions: asking early, who covers travel and accommodation written as questions to discuss (no amounts), the attendants' role on the ground, wellbeing and time off; no packing or fabric advice (owned by the wear page); no travel or legal rules

FAQ of 5 to 7 questions with no amounts, not repeating the wear page's FAQ (e.g. why do we have bridesmaids, what is the difference between a maid and matron of honour, how many bridesmaids should I have, can a man be a bridesmaid, what does a bridesmaid do on the day, do bridesmaids have to travel for a destination wedding)

Internal links: /expert-advice/what-do-bridesmaids-wear (attire, matching dresses, who pays for dresses); /expert-advice/wedding-traditions pillar; /expert-advice/why-do-brides-wear-veils; /expert-advice/something-old-something-new; /trending/whats-inside-rei-germars-bridesmaid-kit once if natural; /magazine; /wonderland-concierge
